title: Stalked for Months, Reported Again and Again: Indian-Origin Woman Shot Dead in Sacramento
excerpt: Shalini Thakur, 38, had told Sacramento deputies about a tracker hidden in her car and secured a restraining order months before she was killed. The suspect was later found dead after a freeway standoff.
body:
• Shalini Thakur, a 38-year-old Indian-origin waitress, was shot and killed on September 8 in a Sacramento parking lot as she arrived for her shift at Panera Bread, after what police describe as months of stalking by an acquaintance.
  • The suspect, 22-year-old Rohit Rohit, was later found dead in his car on Highway 50 after a standoff with deputies, with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office.
  • Thakur had reported the harassment repeatedly since January, found a tracking device hidden in her car, and obtained a restraining order in May that the suspect allegedly violated in July.
  • The U.S. Department of Homeland Security says Rohit entered the country illegally in 2023 and was released pending immigration proceedings, turning the killing into a flashpoint in the debate over enforcement and sanctuary policies.

A 38-year-old Indian-origin woman was shot and killed in Sacramento last week after months of what police describe as escalating stalking by a man she knew from his delivery work — a case that has reignited debate in the United States over both victim protection and immigration enforcement.

Shalini Thakur, who worked as a waitress at an IHOP in Sacramento, was killed on Tuesday, September 8, outside a Panera Bread restaurant in the Arden Arcade shopping plaza, where she had also been working. According to accounts reported by Fox News and the New York Post, a coworker was dropping her off when the suspect approached her in the parking lot. When Thakur tried to run, he chased her, shot her multiple times, and — per the Department of Homeland Security's account — shot her again in the head at close range after she collapsed before fleeing in his car. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

Months of warning signs

The killing came at the end of what the Sacramento County Sheriff's Office describes as a months-long pattern of harassment. Thakur told deputies in January that she had found an Apple AirTag tracking device hidden under the hood of her car. The suspect, 22-year-old Rohit Rohit, knew Thakur from his DoorDash delivery work; she told police he parked outside her home for hours, talked to her daily, and pressed her to marry him.

https://x.com/NalinisKitchen/status/2099005483365621939

According to reporting by Fox News, Rohit deflated her tires so he could show up offering help, tried to stop her from socializing, threatened to shoot himself or anyone she met, and once used a copy of her apartment key to enter her home while she slept — later telling police he was worried because she hadn't answered him.

Thakur initially declined to press charges or seek a restraining order, though deputies stayed in contact with her. In May, after further urging from sheriff's officials, she obtained the order. On July 29, Rohit allegedly violated it by leaving groceries at her front door, according to reports; deputies tried to contact him twice.

"She could have been saved. She told police so many times. She called them, but nobody did anything."

— Sudesh Kumari, Shalini Thakur's mother

"I am alone in this world. Restraining order after restraining order… police did not protect my daughter," Kumari told the New York Post. "She loved them all. She loved everyone."

The suspect's end

After the shooting, investigators tracked Rohit using witness information and license-plate readers, locating him on eastbound Highway 50 near Watt Avenue. A standoff with Sacramento sheriff's deputies shut down the freeway for hours; when deputies finally approached the car, they found Rohit unresponsive in the driver's seat with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Sacramento Sheriff Jim Cooper said he believed the suspect "was headed somewhere else to do someone else harm," according to the New York Post. The sheriff's office said its criminal investigation remains ongoing, though no prosecution is now possible.

Immigration flashpoint

The Department of Homeland Security says Rohit crossed into the United States illegally near Yuma, Arizona, in August 2023, was held at Border Patrol and ICE facilities, and was released in September 2023 under an order of recognizance pending immigration proceedings — after which the department says it never heard from him again.

"This tragedy would have been completely avoided if it weren't for the Biden Administration RELEASING this killer into our country," a DHS spokesperson said, blaming California's sanctuary-state policies, which limit local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Former DHS officials added that Rohit had at least two police contacts before the killing at which he could have been detained for immigration violations.

What it means for the diaspora

For Indian-American families, the case touches two raw nerves at once: the vulnerability of women facing persistent harassment, and the politics of immigration status. Thakur's story — months of documented warnings, a restraining order, an alleged violation — raises the familiar question of whether protective orders and police intervention are enough when an abuser is determined. Meanwhile, the suspect's immigration history has made the killing a talking point in Washington's ongoing fight over enforcement and sanctuary jurisdictions.

What happens next is largely out of the courts' hands: with the suspect dead, there will be no trial. The remaining questions — whether deputies could have acted more aggressively after the July violation, and whether federal detention policies need retooling — will be fought over in public debate rather than in front of a jury.
